````math
#### 4.1.4 Training strategy

The training strategy is identical as described in \[[36](#bib.bib36)\],
using a variant of ORPO \[[53](#bib.bib53)\] and DPO, specifically the
EXO variant \[[54](#bib.bib54), [44](#bib.bib44)\].

### 4.2 Recursive reasoning implementation

We delineate details and prompts used in the recursive reasoning
implementation visualized in
Figure [5](#S2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 2.4 In-situ graph generation and recursive reasoning through multi-agent modeling ‣ 2 Results and Discussion ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR").
The Graph-PRefLexOR recursive reasoning algorithm iteratively refines
graph representations of relational mechanics using a multi-agent system
with Agent \#1 being the Graph Reasoning model, and Agent \#2 being the
non fine-tuned meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct model.

### 4.3 Knowledge garden prompting strategy through agentic modeling

Below is an example of how the knowledge graph is expanded by providing
the set of earlier graph structures (graph_str) and asking another LLM
agent to develop a new question, to which Graph-PReFLexOR then responds,
then generating a new graph. Since the prompt includes the earlier
keywords/nodes as instructed in the prompt, the algorithm results in a
well-connected graph that expands in new directions. The prompt can be
constructed in particular ways to emphasize certain aspects. For this
example, we seek to create multi-disciplinary outputs, especially at the
interface with art.

for this particular prompt.

### 4.4 Graph visualization

We use mermaid.js to visualize graphs, where the output of the graph
reasoning model is converted to the scripting language using Claude 3.5
Sonnet, then exported using the web editor
([https://mermaid.live/](https://mermaid.live/)). Additional
visualizations and analyses are conducted using
Gephi \[[55](#bib.bib55)\] ([https://gephi.org/](https://gephi.org/))
and various plugins therein.

Text Box 3: Result of developed by o1 based on the results developed by
Graph-PReFLexOR, explaining the concept of ‘Mytho-Luminal Liminality’.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
This diagram suggests that “thin places,” though mythic, can motivate
new creative efforts in synthetic biology, while “Challenging
Understanding Boundaries” provides a conceptual conduit that connects
folklore-inspired liminality to biomaterial research. By embedding
*Elastin-Like Proteins* or *Collagen Tripeptides* in immersive artworks,
one effectively fashions a domain where the physical and the
transcendent meet, thus triggering the awe and disorientation
characteristic of thin places. This theoretical approach—*Mytho-Luminal
Liminality*—offers a hitherto unexplored avenue for *transdisciplinary*
collaboration: artistry in living materials that is at once rooted in
ancient mythic boundary concepts, yet forward-looking in its deployment
of cutting-edge biotechnology. Within the broader schema of
Mytho-Luminal Liminality, our knowledge graph highlights that highly
specific molecular elements—such as *Collagen Tripeptide (Gly-X-Y)* and
*Tensin*—“relate to” one another en route to *Protein Design*, an entity
itself classified as a *Biological Molecule*. From a philosophical
vantage, this chain suggests that the *structural elegance* of protein
segments (e.g., the repeating Gly-X-Y motif) can be approached as a
modern instantiation of *boundary-challenging* principles. Indeed, just
as a thin place blurs the division between spiritual and mundane, so too
does *Protein Design* blur the line between “naturally occurring” and
“engineered” molecular architectures. Further underscoring this
parallel, our graph shows that *Molecular Modeling* (an *IS-A*
*Computational Technique*) directly *relates to* both *Collagen* and
*Elastin*, reinforcing the idea that an interplay of *artistic
imagination* and *technical rigor* underlies the creation of new protein
scaffolds. Philosophically, this implies that *challenging our
understanding of boundaries*—which, in mythic contexts, manifests as a
thin place—can also guide transformative science in tissue engineering
and biomaterial innovation. By weaving mythic insights into protein
design thinking, one treats the protein-folding arena as a “liminal
space” where computational, biological, and even artistic considerations
converge to yield novel forms that feel as uncanny and awe-inspiring as
an ancient threshold between worlds.

## Appendix S1 Example: Mapping two distinct, but isomorphic graphs into a shared representation

For sake of the demonstration, we have two distinct graphs that
represent the equations:

|     |                                            |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       G_{1}:F=m\times a,\quad G_{2}:V=I\times R,
       ```                                         |     |

where $`G_{1}`$ and $`G_{2}`$ are defined as detailed below:

##### Graph Structures:

- •
  Graph $`G_{1}`$:

  - –
    Nodes: $`F,m,a,=,\times`$
  - –
    Edges:
    $`=\to F,=\to\times,\times\to m,\times\to a,m\to\times,a\to\times`$
- •
  Graph $`G_{2}`$:

  - –
    Nodes: $`V,I,R,=,\times`$
  - –
    Edges:
    $`=\to V,=\to\times,\times\to I,\times\to R,I\to\times,R\to\times`$

##### Initial Embeddings:

The nodes in $`G_{1}`$ and $`G_{2}`$ are assigned distinct
two-dimensional embeddings to reflect their unique roles in the
equations. The initial embeddings, chosen randomly here, are referred to
as iteration 0 in
Table [S1](#A1.T1 "Table S1 ‣ Initial Embeddings: ‣ Appendix S1 Example: Mapping two distinct, but isomorphic graphs into a shared representation ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR").
Of course, embeddings in a LLM are much higher-dimensional but the 2D
illustration allows us to exemplify the approach more easily. In the
scope of a LLM, the initial embeddings would reflect how tokens are
mapped into the embedding space via the embedding layer from which on
they are processed further.

| Node       | Graph     | Initial Embedding |
|------------|-----------|-------------------|
| $`F`$      | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(0.7,\;0.3)`$   |
| $`m`$      | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(0.6,\;0.9)`$   |
| $`a`$      | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(0.1,\;0.9)`$   |
| $`=`$      | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(1.2,\;0.5)`$   |
| $`\times`$ | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(0.8,\;0.6)`$   |
| $`V`$      | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(0.2,\;0.9)`$   |
| $`I`$      | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(0.05,\;0.8)`$  |
| $`R`$      | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(0.9,\;0.1)`$   |
| $`=`$      | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(1.2,\;0.5)`$   |
| $`\times`$ | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(0.8,\;0.6)`$   |

Table S1: Distinct 2D embeddings (iteration 0) for each variable in
$`G_{1}`$ and $`G_{2}`$. the variables $`F`$, $`m`$, $`a`$, $`V`$, $`I`$
and $`R`$ have different embeddings as they would in a LLM, since each
token is assigned a unique embedding. The embeddings for $`=`$ and
$`\times`$ are identical in both cases, as they would be in a LLM since
the same tokens are mapped to the same vector.

##### Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) Update Mechanism:

For details on GIN models, we refer readers to other
literature \[[56](#bib.bib56), [13](#bib.bib13)\]. For the demonstration
here we assume we have a small MLP with nonlinear activations (ReLU) in
our GIN update:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(k+1)}=\mathrm{MLP}\bigl((1+\epsilon)\cdot\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(k)}+\!\!\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\mathbf{h}_{u}^{(k)}\bigr),
``` |  |

where $`\mathcal{N}(v)`$ are the neighbors of $`v`$, and

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{x})=\sigma\bigl(W_{L}\,\sigma(W_{L-1}\dots\sigma(W_{2}\,\sigma(W_{1}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}_{1})+\mathbf{b}_{2})\dots+\mathbf{b}_{L-1})+\mathbf{b}_{L}\bigr).
``` |  |

Weights/biases $`(W_{1},W_{2},\dots\mathbf{b}_{1},\mathbf{b}_{2},\dots`$
) are learnable parameters optimized during training of the model.

##### Final Embeddings After One Iteration

For the sake of the demonstration, we identified a particular set of
weights and biases such that the embeddings of the distinct variables
are mapped into the same representation by the GIN operation. Hence,
after one iteration of summation and MLP, the updated embeddings
$`\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(1)}`$ are shown in
Table [S2](#A1.T2 "Table S2 ‣ Final Embeddings After One Iteration ‣ Appendix S1 Example: Mapping two distinct, but isomorphic graphs into a shared representation ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR").

| Node | Graph | $`\mathbf{h}_{v}^{(1)}`$ | (Comments) |
|----|----|----|----|
| $`=`$ | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(0.58,\;-0.81)`$ | Matches $`=^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{2}`$ |
| $`F`$ | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(-0.96,\;0.29)`$ | Matches $`V^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{2}`$ |
| $`\times`$ | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(0.39,\;-0.92)`$ | Matches $`\times^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{2}`$ |
| $`m`$ | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(-0.70,\;0.72)`$ | Matches $`I^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{2}`$ |
| $`a`$ | $`G_{1}`$ | $`(0.68,\;0.73)`$ | Matches $`R^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{2}`$ |
| $`=`$ | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(0.58,\;-0.81)`$ | Matches $`=^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{1}`$ |
| $`V`$ | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(-0.96,\;0.29)`$ | Matches $`F^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{1}`$ |
| $`\times`$ | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(0.39,\;-0.92)`$ | Matches $`\times^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{1}`$ |
| $`I`$ | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(-0.70,\;0.72)`$ | Matches $`m^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{1}`$ |
| $`R`$ | $`G_{2}`$ | $`(0.68,\;0.73)`$ | Matches $`a^{(1)}`$ in $`G_{1}`$ |

Table S2: Iteration 1 embeddings after the GIN update with a nonlinear
MLP. Notice that the embeddings for $`G_{1}`$ and $`G_{2}`$ are now
aligned, respecting the functional equivalence of their structures. See
Figure [S3](#A1.F3 "Figure S3 ‣ Discussion ‣ Appendix S1 Example: Mapping two distinct, but isomorphic graphs into a shared representation ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR")
for a plot.

##### Discussion

This example demonstrates the power of GINs in mapping distinct concepts
into a shared representation, forming one example of how abstraction can
be achieved. Despite the graphs $`G_{1}`$ and $`G_{2}`$ starting with
distinct initial embeddings and different structures, the GIN
successfully aligned their embeddings after one iteration. This
alignment reflects the structural equivalence of the graphs:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\textit{isomorphic graphs with equivalent structures}\;\Longrightarrow\;\textit{aligned embeddings}.
``` |  |

Thus, the equations $`F=m\times a`$ and $`V=I\times R`$ share the same
functional relationships
($`\text{output}=\text{parameter}\times\text{input}`$), leading to
aligned embeddings despite differing physical meanings. It confirms that
after processing by the GIN, the two isomorphic graphs have the same
node embeddings and graph-level embeddings.
Figure [S3](#A1.F3 "Figure S3 ‣ Discussion ‣ Appendix S1 Example: Mapping two distinct, but isomorphic graphs into a shared representation ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR")
depicts a visualization of the transformation, including the graphs and
how their embeddings adapt after one layer of GIN.

![Refer to caption](2501.08120v1/Fig_7000.png)

Figure S3: Visualization of transformation of two isomorphic graphs,
each representing an equation ($`F=m\times a`$ and $`V=I\times R`$
(top), into an identical representation (bottom). As one can see, after
the transformation of node embeddings by a GIN, the nodes of both graphs
collapse on the same embeddings are are indistinguishable, to yield a
generalized representation (akin to the concept described in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR"),
bottom). The two graphs not only have the same node embeddings but also
the same graph-level embeddings, revealing that they are isomorphic.

The argument with relation to Graph-PReFLexOR is that rather than
developing a training objective to model isomorphic mappings explicitly,
we model these transformations explicitly by mapping a task into a graph
representation, then a symbolic abstraction, and then to the final
answer, as shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR").
In this visualization, the bottom part of the image particularly shows
how problems are expressed in shared tokenization form to yield
effectively a similar result as visualized in
Figure [S3](#A1.F3 "Figure S3 ‣ Discussion ‣ Appendix S1 Example: Mapping two distinct, but isomorphic graphs into a shared representation ‣ In-situ Graph Reasoning and Knowledge Expansion using Graph-PReFLexOR").
This reflects a mapping into abstraction for generalization and back,
achieving mulitple goals simultaneously.
````
